items.title: $63 Million Family Dollar Settlement: How to Get Your Refund Check
items.summary:
The Federal Trade Commission (FTC) along with 17 states filed a complaint on November 12 alleging that Family Dollar, a nationwide discount retailer, has been overcharging its customers for years. According to the complaint, "Family Dollar routinely charges more at checkout than the prices displayed on its shelves, in its weekly circulars, and on its website and mobile app."

Family Dollar agreed to settle the complaint for $63 million – including $40 million in refunds to eligible customers – and to implement a pricing accuracy program that will be independently reviewed and certified annually. 

For customers who have relied on the discount retailer for low prices on everyday essentials, the news is a sigh of relief as Family Dollar will soon be taking steps to make sure prices are accurate. But it's also a reminder to scrutinize your receipts and be a more skeptical consumer in general. 

What does the FTC complaint against Family Dollar say? The November complaint filed by the FTC cites repeated customer complaints about cashiers and store managers refusing to honor the prices shown on store shelves or in advertisements. This allegedly resulted in millions of dollars in overcharges as customers paid more at checkout than they expected based on advertised prices.

The issue, according to the FTC, stemmed primarily from the retailer's practice of automatically updating prices at the point of sale (the cash register) without ensuring that shelf labels or online list prices had been updated as well. 

But the FTC also cites complaints that Family Dollar frequently refused…
items.t: $63 Million Family Dollar Settlement: How to Get Your Refund Check

items.title: 5 Steps to Take When an Inheritance Causes Anxiety
items.summary:
For many adult children, an inheritance leads to difficult questions about how to spend that money and what would make their parents proud. 

That can cause feelings of anxiety and stress, especially when the inheritance comes as a surprise. 

What heirs often underestimate is how emotionally challenging it can be to make even small, straightforward decisions with that money.

When emotions run high, choosing how to use your inheritance to "do the right thing" can add to the pressure many adult children already feel. But with the right approach, you can create a plan to confidently manage an inheritance — even if you weren't left with instructions on what that might mean. 

Moving past difficult feelings Many adult children who inherit money struggle with grief, guilt and frustration. These emotions can make an inheritance feel like a burden and add to the stress of figuring out how to move forward responsibly. 

Sometimes parents leave their children what's known as a letter of wishes . While it's not a formal legal document, it can provide helpful guidance on how to spend an inheritance without feeling as much guilt and anxiety.

items.title: How Social Security Clawbacks Work After a Death
items.summary:
When a loved one passes away, sorting through their financial estate is often the last thing family members want to manage. However, the Social Security Administration (SSA) operates under a zero-tolerance calendar rule: to legally keep a month's benefit check, you must survive every single second of that calendar month.

If a beneficiary dies on December 31st at 11:59 PM, they did not live through December, and that payment must be returned in full. Because Social Security pays a month in arrears — meaning the payment arriving in January is actually for December — that post-death direct deposit feels like a natural final installment. In reality, it is a government overpayment waiting to be reclaimed.

Here is how the government reclaims your final check, what happens when that money gets accidentally spent and the legal issues most families overlook.

The "must live the entire month" rule 

(Image credit: Getty Images) The foundational rule governing post-death Social Security payments is simple but strict: if a beneficiary passes away on December 30th, they are alive for 30 of the 31 days. Because they did not survive the full calendar month, the SSA treats them as entitled to $0 for December.

Social Security payments are distributed a month behind. The check or direct deposit that lands in an account in January actually represents the benefit for December.

How the money disappears automatically 

(Image credit: Getty Images) You typically do not need to manually write a check to return the funds. As soon as a death is reported (usually by the funeral home or family),…
items.t: How Social Security Clawbacks Work After a Death

Medicare is ending Your spouse is being discharged For them to stay, you must pay When Medicare's limited coverage for nursing home care ends, the couple faces the possibility of paying the national average of almost $10,000 per month out of pocket until they've spent down enough assets to qualify for long-term care Medicaid . 

At that point, many families do exactly what they shouldn't: They begin writing large checks to the nursing home, liquidating investments, moving money around, giving assets to children, or taking the nursing home resident home because they believe they have no alternative.

items.title: How a 721 Exchange Ends the 1031 Merry-Go-Round
items.summary:
Billie was our first 1031 exchange client. 

In 2015 she was 77, a widow with one daughter. She and her late husband had built up several debt-free rental properties over the years, and she was tired of tenants, trash and toilets. Selling outright would have netted about $2.5 million before taxes and about $1.7 million after. 

She didn't want to hand over $800,000 in taxes, so she exchanged into Delaware statutory trusts (DSTs) instead.

She understood the deal going in. Each DST would sell in five to seven years, and she would need to exchange again to keep the tax deferred. That was fine.

In the summer of 2021, the sponsor told us her first DST would sell that November. Billie was 83. The question she brought to our meeting wasn't, "What happened?" She knew exactly what happened. The question was: "I know I can do this again. Do I want to?"

She did not. She still wanted the income. She still wanted real estate. She just didn't want the job, and she didn't want to go shopping for it every five years. So she took about $100,000 out, paid tax on that portion, and put the rest into a DST built to move into a REIT . As her other DSTs come full cycle, they will follow.

Every DST investor eventually asks Billie's question. The strategy she chose at 77 assumed a version of herself that no longer existed. That's why I think you should understand a 721 exchange before doing another 1031 — and ideally before doing your first one.

items.title: What You Will Pay for Medicare in 2027
items.summary:
Medicare premiums and deductibles are rising again in 2027 , making it critical for retirees to review their out-of-pocket costs during open enrollment. While Part A remains premium-free for most beneficiaries , costs for Part B outpatient care, Medicare Advantage plans, and standalone Part D drug coverage will all adjust in the coming year.

Medicare premiums and deductibles are due to increase in 2027 from 2026 levels , with Part B premiums rising by 3.2%. The Part A deductible increased by a smaller amount, 2.3%.

In addition to regular premiums, higher-income beneficiaries may owe an extra monthly surcharge on their Medicare Part B and Part D coverage, known as the income-related monthly adjustment amount ( IRMAA ). In 2027, high earners will pay an extra Part B surcharge of $83.70 to $502.40 on top of the standard Part B premium, plus a monthly Part D surcharge of $15.40 to $96.40. 

Individuals paying the smallest surcharges will owe $3,702 ($7,404 for couples) annually for Part B premiums and Part B and Part D surcharges. Total annual costs at the highest end will be $9,698.40 for individuals and $19,396.80 for couples. 

Whether you rely on original Medicare paired with a Medigap policy or choose a Medicare Advantage (MA) plan, understanding these baseline figures will help you anticipate healthcare expenses and protect your retirement cash flow in 2027.

items.title: Why SNL's Viral 'Sister' Sketch Hit So Close to Home
items.summary:
A viral Saturday Night Live skit called "Sister" is making waves this week — not for taking on politics, but for exposing an uncomfortable truth about how families handle aging parents.

The parody pharma commercial opens with actor John Mulaney playing an earnest son who doesn't want to put his father in a nursing home, but can't afford a home health aide. "That's when I heard about Sister," he says. "Sister is a live-in 24/7 elder care provider that is completely free — and also your sister."

The mock commercial then pivots to the science behind the solution: "Years of internalized sexism warp Sister's brain into thinking caretaking is her responsibility."

A scenario that's all too close to reality The skit drew millions of views because the data behind it isn't funny at all. The National Alliance for Caregiving and AARP say 63 million Americans are providing care today. But 61% of those caregivers are women, compared to 38% of men. 

The report also found that 64% of caregivers experience high emotional stress. Caregivers who feel forced into the role (56% of respondents) have worse mental health outcomes.

The financial toll on caregivers is also real. AARP reports that caregivers could lose $120,500, on average, over their lifetimes due to lost wages and future Social Security benefits. And the Center for the Study of Social Policy says female caregivers 50 and older have 58% less retirement wealth than those who aren't caregivers.

Rob Klein, long-term care planning strategist at CAREfidence , wasn't thrilled with the skit.

"While it got some laughs, it's actually…

items.title: How to Avoid a Mutual Fund Tax Hit at Year-End
items.summary:
Investors are no doubt starting to think about their 2026 taxes, but the company that manages your mutual funds has been focused on the topic for a while. 

As fiscal years wrap up, typically at the end of October, fund companies start calculating how much of their funds’ income and capital gains they’ll distribute to investors before the end of the year. 

If you hold mutual funds in a tax-advantaged account, such as a 401(k) or an IRA, there’s not much to worry about. But if you own a mutual fund in your taxable brokerage account , you’ll owe taxes on that distribution, so it’s best to have a plan.

What often catches investors off guard is that the tax liability crops up even if they don’t buy or sell a fund share over the course of the year. Worse, it’s often the funds that have performed particularly badly during the year that pay outsized distributions. 

"If you’re seeing a big distribution in a down year, that’s just insult added to injury," says Holly Swan , head of wealth solutions at Allspring Global Investments.

It helps to be prepared by knowing more about whether your fund is planning a distribution — and if so, how much — as well as what you can do to minimize your tax bill.

Here’s how it works: When a mutual fund sells a stock, bond, or other investment it owns, it either makes a profit or takes a loss. At the end of the year, if gains outweigh the losses, funds are required to pass that amount to investors. 

The annual distribution also includes income from dividends or interest. Fund shareholders who hold their shares in a taxable account must then pay…
items.t: How to Avoid a Mutual Fund Tax Hit at Year-End

The announcement of state plans to engage with young people told us nothing we hadn’t already heard, but it still felt momentous

It’s one of the country’s worst kept secrets. There can’t be anyone left who hasn’t heard of Alan Milburn’s Neets review, let alone read most of it too. It feels as if it’s become part of the fabric of our society for the past six months. There will be a Neets-shaped hole in our lives when it’s over.

Not a day has gone by without some part of it being leaked to the media. Seldom has a pitch been so icomprehensively rolled. Milburn has been out and about giving interviews to everyone – regardless of whether they wanted one or not. I rather suspect the reason Royal Mail lied about calling to collect my parcel return yesterday was because the driver found himself cornered by Milburn for a couple of hours and was unable to complete his round. Either that, or Royal Mail has a fleet of vans crisscrossing the country whose sole purpose is to make sure they never deliver anything. Ghost vans.

items.title: Dying Rich vs Living Well: Guide to Wise Retirement Spending
items.summary:
For most of our working lives, the financial instructions were pretty simple: 

Earn money Save money Invest money Don't buy something ridiculous because your neighbor bought one Then you retire , and suddenly, the rules change.

You're no longer primarily accumulating money. You're trying to make it last. You're navigating Social Security , Medicare, taxes, required minimum distributions ( RMDs ), inflation, adult children, grandchildren and a seemingly endless parade of people who would be delighted to separate you from your savings.

Welcome to the new economy for older people. And here's the problem: So many financial pundits spend decades teaching people how to save for retirement and remarkably little time teaching them how to manage money once they're actually retired. As a financial literacy expert, that is my focus for this article. 

Here are some rules to keep in mind for your transition from the accumulation phase to the spending phase of retirement.

Rule No. 1: Stop thinking of your nest egg as a pile of money A million dollars sounds like a fortune … until it has to pay you a salary for 25 or 30 years. That's the mental shift retirees need to make. Your IRA isn't a jackpot. It's your personal pension fund.

items.title: IRS Increases 2027 FSA Limits Just in Time for Open Enrollment
items.summary:
With many household budgets stretched thin and medical costs continuing to climb, finding ways to make every paycheck stretch a little further matters more than ever. 

Fortunately, the IRS recently announced new 2027 contribution limits for tax-advantaged healthcare accounts like health flexible spending accounts (FSAs).

With an FSA, employees can make payroll deposits to help pay insurance deductibles or other qualifying medical expenses (including items not covered by insurance). 

And if you participate in one of these accounts, your contributions are tax-free. That means they are generally not subject to federal income tax, Social Security taxes, or Medicare taxes .

However, you cannot exceed the annual contribution limit — your employer's payroll will typically cap your deductions, and any accidental excess (such as from switching jobs mid-year with a dependent care FSA) will be taxed at ordinary federal income tax rates .

But with FSA contributions higher for 2027 than last year, there's much more to know this open enrollment season. Read on.

FSA limits 2027 Flexible spending accounts use your contributions to pay certain out-of-pocket health care costs for yourself, your spouse, and your dependents. As mentioned, the money you chip into the account is tax-free.

If you have an FSA account, here are the maximum amounts you can contribute for 2027 (tax returns normally filed in 2028).

The FSA contribution limit for 2027 is $3,500; that’s up from $3,400 the previous year. If your spouse has a plan through their employer, they may also contribute up to $3,500…
items.t: IRS Increases 2027 FSA Limits Just in Time for Open Enrollment

items.title: Are You Spending Too Little in Retirement? Ask Yourself These 3 Questions
items.summary:
Are you skipping that week-long Mediterranean cruise because gas prices are too high? Passing on dinner out because grocery bills keep climbing? Or holding back because you fear your money won't last thirty years of retirement? 

If so, you're in good company. Millions of retirees are sitting on hard-earned nest eggs, fearing their savings will run dry.

For many, that fear is unfounded. According to research from the Employee Benefit Research Institute, most retirees still have roughly 60% to 70% of their savings left untouched even after two decades in retirement. 

Even if you are legacy-minded and hope to leave an inheritance to your kids, you may have extra money you can spend. Sometimes, permitting yourself to use it comes down to a little soul-searching and smart financial planning.

Are you spending enough in retirement? Ask yourself these three questions:

1. Do I have enough reliable income to cover my expenses? 

(Image credit: Getty Images) Peace of mind is essential in retirement. That's why financial advisers say the first question to ask yourself is simple: Are your basic monthly bills covered? If the answer is yes, you can start opening the purse strings with much more confidence.

"To what degree are the essentials covered with income you can rely on?" says Joseph Sicchitano , head of individual solutions at Principal Financial Group.

Reliable income usually means Social Security , a pension, savings, or some combination of the three. "If your plan can support $6,000 a month and you are getting by nicely on $5,000, then you can probably spend a little bit…
items.t: Are You Spending Too Little in Retirement? Ask Yourself These 3 Questions

items.title: Does Your Car Insurance Cover These 5 Cold-Weather Problems?
items.summary:
Winter is full of hazards for your vehicle. You might wake up after a snowstorm to find a tree branch has fallen on your car. Or you might hit black ice during your commute and slide into a guardrail. 

These situations can cause thousands of dollars in damage, and you might expect your car insurance to cover the expense. But whether your insurer will pay depends on the type of coverage you carry.

Before freezing temperatures and snowy roads become part of your daily routine, take some time to review your policy. Here's a look at five common winter hazards, what your car insurance may cover and where you might have gaps in coverage.

Understand what your car insurance covers before winter weather hits Before winter weather arrives, take a look at your current coverage. Insurers offer three main types of car insurance : 

Liability insurance: Generally required by states, liability coverage pays for injuries and property damage you cause to others in an accident. It doesn't cover damage to your own vehicle. Collision insurance: Collision coverage helps pay to repair or replace your vehicle if you hit another car or object. That may include accidents caused by icy or snowy roads, regardless of whether you're at fault. A deductible typically applies. Comprehensive insurance: Comprehensive insurance covers damage to your vehicle from non-collision events, such as falling branches, hail, theft and certain types of windshield damage. A deductible typically applies. Most states require drivers to carry a minimum amount of liability insurance , but comprehensive and collision…
items.t: Does Your Car Insurance Cover These 5 Cold-Weather Problems?

items.title: Simply telling the AA about my minor no-fault, no-claim prang doubled my insurance quote
items.summary:
A recent £364 renewal quote suddenly increased to an extortionate £796

My car was involved in a minor no-fault accident. The other driver admitted responsibility and said they would pay for repairs without involving insurers. I informed my insurer, the AA, without making a claim. It had recently sent a renewal quote for £364, but after reporting the accident I was sent a revised figure of £796.86.

I was told by a call handler that any insurance company would do the same. However, they eventually lowered the quote to £452.31. This seems extortionate for a no-fault, no-claim prang.

items.title: Raising the state pension age above 70 would harm the poorest | Letters
items.summary:
Joanna Elson of the Independent Age charity is concerned about poverty among pensioners and says ministers need to think hard before making changes

You report (11 November) Torsten Bell’s suggestion that the Conservatives would need to raise the state pension age above 70 to meet the cost of keeping the triple lock.

It is well known that raising the state pension age increases poverty rates among those who have to wait longer for it, with those on the lowest incomes hit the hardest. The Institute for Fiscal Studies reported that when the age rose from 65 to 66, the poverty rate among 65-year-olds more than doubled, with renters and those with lower levels of education among those more likely to struggle.

Continue reading...
items.t: Raising the state pension age above 70 would harm the poorest | Letters
